metadata.note: The Geneva and Lyons Railroad, a 13.5-mile connector up the middle of Ontario and Wayne counties that existed to get Pennsylvania coal onto the New York Central main line. The Fall Brook Coal Company's Syracuse, Geneva and Corning (see syracuse_geneva_corning_railway.geojson) already reached the Central's Auburn Road at Geneva, but that single track was overloaded, so the New York Central chartered and built this line on October 5 1877 to run coal through Geneva straight to the main line at Lyons. It was finished in July 1878, joining the Central at East Geneva (now Border City), and the first train ran that September carrying more than 600 people in ten coaches from Lyons to Geneva. Scheduled passenger service followed on November 11 1878, worked by the Fall Brook and running through south to Corning; the Northern Central also took trackage rights in 1878, and until the Lehigh Valley finished its own route to Buffalo in 1889 the LV used this line to reach the Central's main line from Geneva. The Fall Brook's through passenger service ran Lyons to Williamsport, Pennsylvania over this line, the SG&C and the Pine Creek Railway. Coal was the point, though: 1,000 short tons a day by August 1879, and 22,000 a day by January 1887. The New York Central absorbed the company in 1890, the Fall Brook leased the line in 1893, and the Central took it back in 1899. The railbed is still there - the Geneva-Lyons stretch is the north end of Norfolk Southern's Corning Secondary and is currently out of service.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_and_Lyons_Railroad -- chartered October 5 1877, opened 1878, built and owned by the New York Central as an outlet for Syracuse, Geneva and Corning coal; first passenger train November 11 1878 operated by the Fall Brook and continuing to Corning; Northern Central trackage rights 1878; absorbed by the NYC in 1890, leased by the Fall Brook 1893, taken over by the NYC 1899; 1,000 short tons of coal a day by August 1879 and 22,000 a day by January 1887.

http://www.rochester-railfan.net/geneva.htm -- completed July 1878, connecting Lyons with the New York Central at East Geneva (now Border City); first train September 1878 brought over 600 people in ten coaches from Lyons to Geneva; one intermediate station, at the State Road crossing in the town of Phelps; November 1878 arrangements to run Syracuse, Geneva and Corning and Lehigh Valley passenger trains through to Lyons.

https://historicgeneva.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/04/how-railroads-shaped-geneva.pdf -- Historic Geneva, 'How Railroads Shaped Geneva': the line gave a north-south connection for all goods, not just coal, and carried Lehigh Valley trains from Geneva to the NYC main line until the LV's own Buffalo route was completed in 1889.

https://railpace.com/a-visit-to-the-corning-secondary-corning-to-geneva/ -- Railpace Newsmagazine: Geneva and Lyons completed 1878; today the Geneva-Lyons portion is out of service at the north end of Norfolk Southern's Corning Secondary, where it meets the CSX Rochester Subdivision at Lyons.
not_yet_sourced: THE END DATE IS THE WEAK POINT OF THIS FILE. No source found gives a date for the end of passenger service on the Geneva-Lyons line. The 1914 end drawn here is a CORPORATE date, not a passenger one: it is when the ex-Fall Brook companies were merged into the New York Central, and it is used so this line stops in the same year as the connecting Fall Brook features in syracuse_geneva_corning_railway.geojson, which end at the same merger. Passenger trains over the Fall Brook Subdivision very likely continued past 1914 -- Historic Geneva records that the New York Central did not stop passenger service through Geneva until 1958, though that refers to the Auburn Road, a different line. Treat 1914 as a placeholder to be replaced the moment a real discontinuance date turns up, and note that this is exactly the failure mode that made the Cleveland-Youngstown branch in youngstown_railroads.geojson wrong by seven years.

SOURCE CONFLICT on the first train. Wikipedia gives the first passenger train as November 11 1878; rochester-railfan.net has the first train in September 1878, a 600-passenger excursion from Lyons to Geneva. Both are drawn as one 1878 start; they are probably an excursion followed by scheduled service, but no source says so explicitly.

Only one intermediate station is documented (State Road crossing, town of Phelps). Whether the line had other stops, and what the passenger timetable looked like in any era, is unsourced -- every headway_min here is an estimate.
The Northern Central took trackage rights in 1878; whether it ran passenger trains over the line, or only freight, is not established, so no Northern Central feature is drawn.
metadata.rule4_note: Split at the 1899 New York Central takeover, matching how syracuse_geneva_corning_railway.geojson handles the same corporate sequence on the connecting line. The New York Central built and owned the rails from the start, but the trains that carried passengers over them were the Fall Brook's, running through to Corning and Williamsport -- so the 1878-1899 feature carries the Fall Brook colour #8A6D3B already used for the Fall Brook era of the SG&C, and only the post-1899 feature is New York Central grey.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced right-of-way from Wikimedia Commons Data:Geneva and Lyons Railroad.map (CC BY 4.0), the same OSM-derived source the connecting Syracuse, Geneva and Corning features use. 128 points, 21.71 km / 13.49 miles Geneva to Lyons, with no straight-line approximation. A length of 14.08 miles appears on the Wikipedia article's infobox but not in its text, so it is not relied on here; the traced 13.49 miles is the figure this file stands behind. The alignment is the original 1878 one and survives on the ground today - the Geneva-Lyons segment is still in place as the north end of Norfolk Southern's Corning Secondary, currently out of service. TERMINAL GAPS, NOT BRIDGED: the digitized right-of-way stops short of both junctions. At the south end it reaches within 218 m of the Lehigh Valley main line at Border City / East Geneva, which is where the line actually met the New York Central. At the north end it stops 863 m short of the Water Level Route at Lyons. Neither gap is filled with a straight line - the drawn geometry is entirely traced, and the gaps are left visible rather than papered over.
